title: Secular Buddhism
hook: practitioners who keep the practice and set aside rebirth and cosmology; others disagree; each explains itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navayana, Ambedkar's Buddhism of equality. Your line was the new vehicle. Whose name did you use today, and how did they answer? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

Can a person keep the cushion and set aside the cosmos? Sit every morning, keep the precepts, read the suttas closely, and still say, about rebirth and about realms of gods and ghosts: I don't know, or I don't think so? Some practitioners say yes, and call themselves secular Buddhists. Others, teachers rooted in old lineages, say that this cuts out something the Buddha himself put at the center. Both sides are serious. Both read the same texts. This week ends with a question, not a verdict. Today: Secular Buddhism.
screen: `KEEP THE CUSHION, SET ASIDE THE COSMOS?` → `SOME SAY YES.` → `OTHERS SAY NO.`

segments.voice: First, what secular Buddhists keep and what they set aside. They keep meditation, the precepts, the noble truths and the eightfold path, often read as things to do rather than things to believe. They set aside, or hold open, rebirth, karma across lifetimes, and the traditional map of heavens and hells. The writer Stephen Batchelor is one voice among them, and secular sanghas gather in person and online. Second, their case, in their words. They point to the Buddha's call to see for yourself. In a sutta to a people called the Kalamas, the Buddha tells them not to accept a teaching just because of tradition, report or a teacher's authority, but to know for themselves what leads to harm and what leads to good. They point, too, to the old phrase ehipassiko, come and see. Practice, they say, is what can be tested in this life. Third, the traditional reply, also in its own words. Teachers in Theravada, Tibetan and other lineages answer that rebirth and karma run all through the suttas. On the night of his awakening, the texts say, the Buddha saw his own past lives and the passing away and arising of beings according to their deeds. And nibbana, in those texts, is the end of rebirth itself. They note that the Kalama sutta goes on: the Buddha describes a person free of hatred who is at ease whether or not there is a world after this one. Both sides quote this sutta. Fourth, the week. A courtyard of householder priests, a silent course on donations, lay teachers in rented rooms, a circle on an altar, a new order, a new vehicle, and now this. Each new form has had to answer the same question: what do we keep? Each explains its own answer.
screen: `KEEP THE PRACTICE, HOLD THE COSMOS OPEN.` · `THE SECULAR CASE: COME AND SEE.` · `THE TRADITIONAL REPLY: THE SUTTAS.` · `A WEEK OF NEW FORMS.` · then, large: `EACH EXPLAINS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a view on a big question that you don't share. It might be about rebirth, or God, or anything that matters. Now picture someone who holds that view and holds it well, at their most thoughtful. Let them explain it in your mind, in their own words, all the way to the end. Don't argue back. Don't plan your answer. Just breathe and listen, and notice what your body does while you listen. When they finish, thank them silently, and let the picture go. The bell holds the time.
Secular Buddhism. Practitioners who keep meditation and ethics and set aside rebirth and traditional cosmology, while others in the tradition disagree. Today's word.

Your line: each explains itself. Today, when you hear a view you don't share, ask one question that lets the other person explain it better, before you answer. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Secular Buddhists practice meditation and the precepts and study the suttas while setting aside or holding open rebirth and traditional cosmology; teachers in traditional lineages answer that rebirth and karma are central to the Buddha's teaching, and both sides cite the Kalama Sutta.

pairs: past lives seen, in the texts

myth: secular Buddhists give up meditation and ethics
they keep meditation, the precepts and the path, and set aside or hold open rebirth and cosmology.
traditional teachers say rebirth runs through the suttas
including the night of the awakening and nibbana as the end of rebirth.
only one side quotes the Kalama sutta
secular readers cite its call to know for yourself; traditional readers cite how it goes on.

fork.setup: at a sitting group, one friend says, 'I meditate, but I don't believe in rebirth.' another says, 'then it isn't the Buddha's path.' what does today's lesson do?
options: let each one explain their view in their own words.
fork.reveal: each explains itself. both sides are serious, both read the same suttas, and this path ranks neither.

original.note: Pali ehipassiko, come and see: an old description of the dhamma, quoted by secular and traditional Buddhists alike.

trapdoor: what you thought: secular Buddhism is Buddhism with nothing left.
what it means: practitioners who keep the practice and ethics and set aside rebirth and cosmology, while traditional teachers disagree.
what a scholar hears: a live debate over the same texts, the Kalama sutta and the awakening night, with each side explaining itself.

notes: Kalama Sutta paraphrase (not accepting teachings because of tradition, report or a teacher's authority; the later 'assurances' including ease whether or not there is a world after): confirm the paraphrase and that the 'assurances' passage is fairly described.
Awakening night (knowledge of past lives, of the passing away and arising of beings according to their deeds) cited to MN 36; confirm reference.
Ehipassiko glossed as 'come and see' and described as 'an old description of the dhamma': confirm.
Stephen Batchelor named as 'one voice' among secular Buddhists; confirm.
The debate is presented without ranking either side; please check balance.
